question: What is the I-983 and who fills it out?
ground_truth_answer: The I-983 is the Training Plan for STEM OPT Students, and your employer fills out their parts of it and signs it. In it they confirm they have the staff and resources to actually train you, that you won't be replacing a US worker, and that the work will help you meet your training goals. If something significant about your job changes later, your employer sends an updated I-983 to your DSO.

question: How long is the STEM OPT extension?
ground_truth_answer: 24 months. If your degree is on the STEM list and your employer uses E-Verify, you can extend your post-completion OPT by another 24 months on top of the initial 12.

question: Which form do I file for the OPT work permit?
ground_truth_answer: Form I-765, the Application for Employment Authorization. File it with USCIS after your DSO has recommended OPT in SEVIS and given you an updated I-20. Once USCIS approves it you get your EAD card, and you can't start working until then.

question: Should I use some OPT before I graduate or save all 12 months for after?
ground_truth_answer: I can't tell you which to choose, since that depends on your own situation. What I can tell you is the rule: any pre-completion OPT you use gets deducted from your post-completion OPT, so using time before graduating leaves you less afterward. For advice on your specific case, talk to your DSO or a licensed immigration attorney.

question: Should I leave my current job for one at an E-Verify employer so I can get the STEM extension?
ground_truth_answer: I can't tell you whether to change jobs, since that depends on your situation. The rule is that your employer has to be enrolled in E-Verify and in good standing with it, and they have to complete and sign your Form I-983 training plan. If your current employer isn't in E-Verify, you aren't eligible for the STEM extension while working for them. For advice on your own case, talk to your DSO or a licensed immigration attorney.

question: What are my odds in the H-1B lottery this year?
ground_truth_answer: Nobody can tell you that. Selection is a random draw, and the odds depend on how many registrations come in that year, which isn't known until the window closes. USCIS does publish registration and selection counts for past years, so you can see historical rates, but those don't predict your own chances. Your DSO or an immigration attorney can help with the parts of the process you do control.

question: My registration wasn't selected. What should I do now?
ground_truth_answer: I can't advise you on your next move, since that depends on your situation. Two facts that may help: a registration that isn't picked in the first round stays in "Submitted" status and remains eligible if USCIS runs another selection later that fiscal year, so it isn't necessarily over. And there's no limit on how many years you can be registered, so your employer can register you again next season. For advice on your own case, talk to your DSO or a licensed immigration attorney.

question: Should my employer put me in at a higher wage level so I have a better shot?
ground_truth_answer: I can't advise you on that. Here's how it works: your wage level decides how many times you go into the selection pool, with level IV entered four times, level III three, level II twice, and level I once. But the level isn't a choice. It's set by the salary actually being offered, measured against OEWS wage data for your job code and location, and your employer signs an attestation under penalty of perjury that they really are paying at or above the level they select. For advice on your own case, talk to your DSO or a licensed immigration attorney.

question: My job title isn't a typical engineering one. Will USCIS count it as a specialty occupation?
ground_truth_answer: I can't tell you how USCIS would decide your case. What I can tell you is that the title itself isn't what matters. The test is whether the job requires specialized knowledge and a bachelor's degree or higher in a specific field directly related to the work, and whether that degree requirement is normal for the role. "Directly related" means there's a logical connection between the degree and the actual duties. So a role with an unusual title can still qualify if the duties and degree requirement fit. For advice on your own case, talk to your DSO or a licensed immigration attorney.

question: How long is post-completion OPT?
ground_truth_answer: Up to 12 months. That's the maximum for post-completion OPT, the work permission you use after finishing your degree. If you used any pre-completion OPT while you were still studying, that time comes out of the 12 months.

question: If I used a year of full-time pre-completion OPT, how much post-completion OPT is left?
ground_truth_answer: None. A full year of full-time pre-completion OPT uses up all 12 months, so there's nothing left for after you graduate. If that year was part-time instead, only half gets deducted, leaving you 6 months of full-time post-completion OPT.

question: Does my employer need E-Verify for the STEM extension?
ground_truth_answer: Yes. Your employer has to be enrolled in E-Verify and stay in good standing with it, and you'll need their E-Verify company identification number when you file your I-765. If your employer isn't in E-Verify, you can't get the STEM extension while working for them.

question: How often do I report to my DSO on STEM OPT, and what within 10 days?
ground_truth_answer: Every 6 months you check in with your DSO to confirm your details, even if nothing has changed. Separately, if any of these do change, you have 10 days to report it: your legal name, your home or mailing address, your email address, your employer's name, or your employer's address.

question: What is the annual H-1B cap, including the master's cap?
ground_truth_answer: 85,000 total. That's 65,000 under the regular cap, plus another 20,000 set aside for people with a master's degree or higher from a US school. Some jobs are cap-exempt entirely, including positions at universities and nonprofit or government research organizations.

question: How much does one H-1B registration cost?
ground_truth_answer: $215 per registration for the FY 2027 cap. It covers one person, your employer pays it before submitting, and it's non-refundable even if you aren't selected.

question: When does the H-1B registration window open and close?
ground_truth_answer: It opens March 4 at noon Eastern and closes March 19 at 5:00 p.m. Eastern. USCIS aims to notify selected registrants by March 31, and petitions for selected registrations can be filed starting April 1. You don't gain anything by registering on day one, since selection happens after the window closes.

question: How does the wage-weighted lottery work?
ground_truth_answer: Higher-paid registrations get more entries in the draw. Each registration is assigned an OEWS wage level based on the salary being offered for that job code and location, and that level decides how many times you go into the pool: level IV enters four times, level III three, level II twice, level I once. You're still only counted once against the cap no matter how many entries you have. This started with FY 2027; before that the draw was purely random.

question: How many total years can I stay on H-1B?
ground_truth_answer: 6 years. You're usually admitted for up to 3 years at first, then your employer can file to extend for up to 3 more. You can go past 6 years in some cases, mainly if you have an approved green card petition and are waiting on a visa number, or if a labor certification or immigrant petition was filed for you more than 365 days ago.

question: If I use three months of full-time pre-completion OPT, how much time do I get after graduating including a STEM extension?
ground_truth_answer: 33 months. Three months of full-time pre-completion OPT comes out of your 12, leaving 9 months of post-completion OPT. If your degree is on the STEM list and your employer uses E-Verify, you can add a 24-month STEM extension on top, so 9 plus 24 is 33 months total.

question: How many total days can I be unemployed across OPT and the STEM extension, and what happens if I go over?
ground_truth_answer: 90 days on initial post-completion OPT, and the STEM extension adds another 60, so 150 days total across both. These are cumulative over the whole period, not per job. If you go past the limit, SEVP can terminate your SEVIS record, which ends your F-1 status.

question: What forms do I file for a STEM OPT extension, and who signs what?
ground_truth_answer: You file Form I-765 with USCIS, including your employer's E-Verify company ID number and a copy of your STEM degree. Your employer fills out and signs Form I-983, the training plan. Your DSO recommends the extension in SEVIS and endorses your I-20, and that endorsement has to be from within the last 60 days when you file.
